maintopic: IMPERIAL CONFERENCE

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: IMPERIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the morning press there is an announcement that this year there is to be an Imperial Conference of the nature of that in 1921 to be held simultaneously with an Imperial Economic Conference, and that to the former all prime ministers are invited and all are going save the Prime Minister of New Zealand, who presumably along with the others is to attend the latter. May I ask if this conference has been decided upon if it is to be attended by the Prime Minister or by others of the government, and if so, what is the agenda that has been agreed upon or submitted to the government as subjects for consideration at the economic conference and also at the conference of the character of that of 1921?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: IMPERIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I might say to my right
hon. friend that the report as it appears in the press this morning is correct. An Imperial Conference similar to the one held in 1921 is to be held in London in October simultaneously with an Imperial Economic Conference.

It is hoped that when October comes the expressed wish of the British Prime Minister that the prime ministers of the different dominions should attend the conference may be complied with so far as Canada is concerned.
As to the agenda, I think I might promise my right hon. friend that I will be in a position to place on the Table such papers as we have already received in that connection. Broadly, as to the agenda of the conference of prime ministers, it is similar to the agenda of the conference which my right hon. friend himself attended. The agenda in complete form is not available as yet. It is open to the different governments concerned to make suggestions as to matters to be taken up between now and the time of the conference.
As to the Imperial Economic Conference, The agenda I think is set forth in completer form, and I shall have pleasure in placing on the table of the House the data the government has.

maintopic: IMPERIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Can that data be placed on the Table to-morrow or this week?
Mr. MACKENZIE KING In this, as in alt matters between the Home government and our own, I wish to follow the customary practice of communicating with the British government before I take any action. I shall ask for permission to bring the papers down at an early date.

maintopic: IMPERIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: There can be no possible exception taken that would be acceptable to this House, no possible reason for secrecy in regard to the agenda of either conference.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
Before the motion is put, there is a matter of great urgency which I should like to bring to the attention of the House. It deals with one Mr. John J. Hayes of Calgary. I want first briefly to state this man's position.
Mr. Hayes has been a postal employee of the Dominion of Canada for thirty-three years. Not only has Tie served in that capacity for that length of time, but he also served overseas for some years. After returning he was moved from the Toronto post office to the post office of the city of Calgary. He was moved there immediately after the postal strike in Calgary. He was considered to be of such efficiency that he was placed in the position of supervisor of the letter carriers there at that time. Now for some reason unknown to me, the postmaster at Calgary seemed to take an aversion to Mr. Hayes, and recently they set a trap to catch him. There had been some petty thieving going on in the post office, and a trap was set by a policeman and an official of the post office expressly to catch Mr. Hayes. These gentlemen were in the office watching for Mr. Hayes to put his foot into the trap. They sprang the trap when they were ready but they did not catch Mr. Hayes in it; the money they had planted was found elsewhere. Nevertheless Mr. Hayes was arrested. He was not accorded trial by a jury but was brought before Hon. Mr. Justice McCarthy, and was found guilty. His case then came before the Appeal Court and was heard by Hon. Mr. Justice Beck, Hon. Mr. Justice Hyndman, and Hon. Mr. Justice Clarke, the result being that the conviction was quashed. I would refer those who are interested in the case to the report of the proceedings to be found in Canadian Criminal Cases, volume 38, page 348. Mr. Hayes then found himself a free man. The case was thrown out by the Appeal Court because the evidence against him was insufficient. Subsequently Mr. Hayes applied for reinstatement in the post office but was told by the postmaster that he would have to wait for some time. After repeated attempts to be reinstated he was informed that an order in council had been passed by the present government discharging him from the service, the letter from the Deputy Postmaster General stating that they were taking this action in the light of the judgment as summed up by the dissenting judge of the Appeal Court. I would like to know by what authority the Deputy Postmaster General sets himself above the Appeal Court in this case or, for that matter, by what authority the cabinet even judges a man over the head of the courts.
I want next to show what these proceedings mean to Mr. Hayes himself. As already pointed out he has seen thirty-three years' service. I think his service overseas counted for something more than the regular time, which would give him about thirty-five years' service under the postal department. Now,

Dismissal of John J. Hayes
by his discharge Mr. Hayes loses the pension which rightfully belongs to him as an employee of the department. In this regard I want to point out that on the morning of his arrest the postmaster at Calgary offered Mr. Hayes the privilege of resigning. Had he resigned at that time he would have obtained his pension, but he would not resign because to do so would have been an admission, inferentially at least, that he was guilty of the charge laid against him. Mr. Hayes would not take that opportunity of getting out, but went to the court with his case. However, although he won out in the courts he was summarily dismissed by an order in council. By that dismissal the fruit of his labours of thirty-three to thirty-five years was lost and he himself, as long as the attitude of the department is what it is, is even regarded by his friends with suspicion. I saw Mr. Hayes when I was at Calgary a few days ago and he is undoubtedly in dire financial straits, and his family, at the present time, are dependent upon the precarious charity of friends. Owing to this charge against him, and to the attitude of the department, Mr. Hayes is unable, to get work and is on the very verge of starvation. Now, I submit that a grave injustice has been done to this man. I do not mean to say that the government would knowingly pass an order in council calculated to inflict injustice upon anybody. At the same time, I want to say, that in my opinion, the attitude of the Deputy Postmaster General is contemptible; I cannot find words with which to express my contempt for his attitude in the matter. I imagine that the government reached the decision which it did under the influence of communications received from the postmaster of Calgary, and has not been guided in its decision in this matter by the judgment of the courts. I therefore think this injustice should be remedied. The thirty-three years of creditable service by Mr. Hayes should not be forgotten. The government's attitude not only robs Mr. Hayes of the pension which he has earned, but it also robs him of his character, for it was on the charge of theft that he was discharged, the judgment of the courts notwithstanding.	I would
therefore urge remedial action on the part of the government immediately.	I contend
that Mr. Hayes should be paid his wages from the moment he was arrested until he is reinstated, or else, if the department does not want to reinstate him he should be granted his pension. The least the government can possibly do, in recognition of his service overseas, and of his long term in the service of the department, is to give him his pension.
fMr. Irvine.]

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend to wThat pension he refers-this man's pension as an employee of the government or his pension for service as a soldier overseas?

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
I refer to the pension which Mr. Hayes has earned under the regulations governing postal employees. The man is innocent in the opinion of the court; he has been discharged as innocent of the crime of which he was accused. Therefore, I submit, he ought to receive his pension. He is an honest man in the opinion of the courts, consequently I do not see why anyone should desire to treat him as a criminal. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Shaw):
That all the words after the word "that" to the end of the question be struck out and the following words be inserted instead thereof:
That this House desires to record its opinion that the dismissal of John J. Hayes, formerly employed as a civil servant by the Post Office department, Calgary, Alberta, is wholly unjustifiable, and that immediate steps be taken to redress the injury done to the said John J. Hayes.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Acting Postmaster General):	Mr. Speaker, this
amendment came into my hands just as I was entering the House, and you can readily understand that I have not had time to digest the details of this case. I might point out, however, that if the mail matter, either social or business, is not safe in the hands of public servants, then the business of Canada, as well as our social relations, goes to pieces. Any man who cannot be trusted to handle the mail matter in a post office, while he may have the sympathy, cannot have the confidence, of the people of this country. I do not want to say anything to hurt Mr. Hayes' feelings, and I think bringing up this resolution, while it is in order, is not doing Mr. Hayes a kindness. It would have been better, I think, for my hon. friend to have discussed it with me, to see if there was not some other way of reaching a conclusion. However, I am not responsible for that.
In reference to the charge against Mr. Hayes I may say that he was arrested on September 14th, 1922, charged, first, with stealing a post letter containing $2, a test letter prepared by the investigating officer, contrary to section 364 of the Criminal Code, and stealing a post letter addressed to Mrs. C. I. McFarlane, Calgary, contrary to section 364 of the Criminal Code. One can readily understand that the officials of the post office, particularly the postmaster who is responsible would be in a very embarrassing position, having discovered that at different times, on sundry occasions, letters mailed and contain-

Dismissal of John J. Hayes
ing money had gone astray, and he set out to find who was responsible for this loss of money, and who was guilty of malfeasance in office. He came to the conclusion, with the other officers of the department and officials who were there, that they should investigate the matter. Mr. Hayes was under suspicion at least. This case was tried before Mr. Justice McCarthy. Practically every man in this House knows Mr. Justice McCarthy, who was formerly a member of this House. He heard all the evidence, saw the demeanour of the witnesses, was in a position to take into account all the local conditions and he found Mr. Hayes guilty and sentenced him to three years' imprisonment on each of the two counts, sentences to run concurrently. An appeal was taken. That appeal was heard before three judges; two of them upheld the appeal, one dissenting, Mr. Justice Clarke.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: Did Mr. Justice Clarke dissent?

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: Yes. I must not comment on the judgment-but perhaps I might as well. I will be very delicate about it. Mr. Justice Clarke was at one time a member of this House, and one of the ablest lawyers in the Dominion of Canada, and one of the ablest men that ever sat in this House.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
And appointed by the
late government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: An exception which proves the rule.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
That may have been a
lapse of memory. But we are all unanimous in the opinion that Mr. Justice Clarke is a very able man. An appeal was taken. There were two questions at issue; first, the riglqt of trial by jury, which had been refused at the time of the trial by the presiding judge. My hon. friend for Calgary (Mr. Irvine) referred to that. As a matter of fact, the law provides for the trial, as it took place, without a jury. The second point was insufficient evidence. Two of the judges held that the evidence was not conclusive. Without criticizing the judgment at all, and I am not doing that, I would say that in order to come to a conclusion some other theory must be adopted, or some other explanation must be accepted as to the method by which Mr. Hayes got the letters and money into his possession. One of these was purely presumptive. The first suggestion was that the test letter had been stolen by a letter carrier who had later turned the money in to Hayes when buying stamps. Some letter carrier other than Hayes must have stolen this letter, brought it back
and turned it in to Hayes for stamps-a roundabout proceeding. The second point was that Mr. Tingle substituted this money while he was taking the requisition handed in by Hayes to the clerk from whom he obtained the stamps.
Now certainly the evidence may not have been conclusive, but to my mind the reasoning of the other judges was far from conclusive. I want to point out what Mr. Justice Clarke said in his dissenting judgment. Referring to these two contentions, or suggestions as to the method by which Hayes might have got these letters and this money, Mr. Justice Clarke first deals with the opportunity a letter carrier would have to steal this letter and shows that while it would not have been impossible for a letter carrier to have done it, it was highly improbable. He pointed out that Mr. Hayes's desk was only a few feet from the case in which the letters, including the stolen letters, were placed for his attention. Hayes personally took the letters from the pigeon hole, containing the "removed" letters, and put them on his desk to check them over as usual and turn them over to Clerk Black, the supervisor of city sortation. When examined by Black one of the test letters was there, and the other one was missing. The accused left the room for about 15 or 20 minutes-this was about 8.50 a.m.-immediately after he had turned the letter over to Black. About 9.30 a.m. he sent his assistant, Tingle, with the requisition for postage due stamped to the amount of $3.75, to the stamp vendor on the mezzanine floor. The marked money contained in the missing test letter was found among the moneys sent by Mr. Hayes for stamps. Hayes alleged he got this money from the letter carriers. I am not going to refer further to this judgment, but Mr. Justice Clarke dissented very strongly, giving, to my mind, real reasons for every point of his dissent. We begin with this again: Letters and moneys were found in the possession of Hayes illegally. Mr. Justice McCarthy, who heard all the evidence, sentenced Hayes to three years' imprisonment on each count.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: The minister said that the money and the letters which did not belong to Mr. Hayes, were found in his possession. I think the minister is in error as to that. I do not think any money was found in Mr. Hayes' possession.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
The memorandum which I have here says that Hayes was charged with:
1. Stealing a post letter containing two dollars (test letter prepared by investigating officer) contrary to section 364 (c) of the Criminal Code, and

Dismissal of John J. Hayes
2. Stealing a post letter addressed to Mrs. C. I. McFarlane, Calgary; contrary to section 364 (b) of the Criminal Code.
Hayes appeared before Judge McCarthy and was found guilty and sentenced to three years' imprisonment on each of the two counts.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: That is the charge, but that does not prove that money that did not belong to Mr. Hayes was found in his pockets by the trap-springers.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
Let me read again a synopsis of what Mr. Justice Clarke says:
The carrier would have had to pick out this particular letter from the thirty or more letters in the pigeon hole, which he would have no knowledge of, abstract the money-two dollars, and then turn in the money in two instalments to Hayes in purchasing a few cents worth of stamps, all before 8.50.
From that I take it for granted that the money was found in the possession of Mr. Hayes. But let me get back. I am not going to take the place of the court. Hayes was charged with stealing money and mail matter; Mr. Justice McCarthy, who heard all the evidence, found him guilty and sentenced him to two terms of three years' imprisonment, the terms to run concurrently. The case was taken in appeal on two points: First, refusal of trial by jury. That has been cleared up by Mr. Justice Clarke, who pointed out that the law provides for such trials without a jury. The second was that the evidence was not sufficient. The judges rather took the ground " not conclusive What I have read from the synopsis of the judgment of Mr. Justice Clarke would lead me to believe there was a wide divergence of opinion in that regard. Leaving all that aside, however, this is a man who is under suspicion sufficiently strong to make him a man not worthy to handle the mail of the people of Canada. WTould any man in this House trust a public servant who had been tried and found guilty by Mr. Justice McCarthy and who, although he won on appeal, had applied to the case the remarks of Mr. Justice Clarke which I have read? I cannot but oppose this motion. I am willing to discuss this matter in. the Post Office Department with my hon. friend; but I can assure him and assure Mr. Hayes that the object of the Post Office Department of the Dominion of Canada is not to persecute anybody; its chief object is to have the people of this country served, not only efficiently, but honestly.
Mr. JOS. T. SHAW (Calgary West): Mr. Speaker, I must confess that I am amazed by the attitude assumed by the Acting Postmaster General (Mr. Graham) in connection with this matter. He spent a good deal of time reviewing the judgments of the court and explaining why the view expressed by
[Mi. Graham.]
Mr. Justice Clarke must be upheld. Then, in the next breath, he tells us that he does not want to go into the matter as regards the courts. There can be no question of this fact -John J. Hayes is innocent of the charge which was laid against him.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: Who told the hon. member?

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
There can be no question about that. The courts have decreed that the charges which were laid against Hayes were unfounded, and he stands to-day before the people of Canada and in the eyes of the law an innocent man.
May I say at the outset, that of the questions which were considered by the Court of Appeal in this matter, one was a legal question as to the right of an accused person charged under the section dealing with post office offences, of securing a jury. On that point, the court did not come to any conclusion, because in view of the facts they deemed it unnecessary to consider that question. There were I believe, at least, three questions reserved. The second was: Was the finding against the weight of evidence? That is the question submitted by Mr. Justice McCarthy to the Appellate Court. I think we should have in mind that well-established principle that no man shall be convicted if there is any reasonable doubt as to his guilt. The second question concerned itself with the question of whether or not Mr. Justice McCarthy, in trying the case, had, so to speak, misdirected himself. The third question is:
Did I err in finding the appellant guilty of the charge of stealing from the post office at Calgary a post letter addressed to Mrs. C. I. McFarlane, in that the appellant alleges no guilty intent was established.
Next,
Did I err in failing to direct that no evidence was produced to prove the value of the letter forming the substance of the first charge?
Next,
Did I err in failing to direct that no evidence was produced to prove the value of the letter forming the substance of the second charge?
These questions were placed for consideration before the appellate division, and I want to read some extracts from the judgments of Mr. Justice Beck and Mr. Justice Hyndman, dealing with this matter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: Would the hon. member tell us briefly the decision of the Appellate Court on the second question.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
I am going to read some extracts taken from the judgments of these Appeal Court judges. The judgments themselves are rather long. Mr. Justice Beck

Dismissal oj John J. Hayes
states, and his statement will be found at page 349, Canadian Criminal Cases, volume 38:
As I am of opinion that the conviction must be set aside and the accused discharged upon a proper view of the evidence and the judge's reasons for his decision, I refrain from a consideration of the question whether or not the accused was entitled to be tried by a jury.	[DOT]
Further on at page 354, he continues:
There is absolutely no direct evidence of the guilt of the accused. The evidence against him, such as it is, is wholly inferential. The evidence makes it quite clear to me that, without discrediting in the slightest degree the evidence of Black, Hale, or the constable-
And these, by the way, may I mention, are the gentlemen who framed up the scheme on this particular man:
-(I emphasize this for reasons which will appear later,) there is room for more than one reasonable hypothesis to account for the two marked one-dollar bills being found in the way described in the hands of Hazleton. I set forth these hypotheses, of course, without wishing to suggest guilt on any particular individual.
In other words, Mr. Justice Beck found, under the circumstances, that any one of a number of individuals might have committed the offence. At page 357 Mr. Justice Beck again says:
Applying these principles to the evidence I am convinced not only that had I been trying the case I should not have convicted the accused, but that, in view of the several hypotheses consistent with his innocence, there is no evidence on which he could be properly convicted. Apart from this it seems quite clear to me that the judge misdirected himself. He gave reasons for convicting the accused as follows in which I insert comments indicating which I think are objectionable features.
To my mind it is impossible, in view of the law as I have indicated it, to say that this statement by the trial judge does not indicate that he very seriously misdirected himself. This being so, in my opinion, the conviction cannot stand. If this were the only ground for quashing the conviction, of course the court would have to consider whether or not a new trial should be directed,-
And I direct the attention of the Acting Postmaster General to this:
-but in view of what I have said with reference to the evidence, I would, even if it is thought that the evidence would on a strict application of legal principles justify a conviction, I would refuse to direct a new trial.
In other words, the court is satisfied that if a new trial were directed in this particular case this man must necessarily be found innocent of the charge. Mr. Justice Hyndman also deals with the matter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: The result of the appeal was, then, that the conviction was set aside and a new trial refused.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
Yes. I may remark, for the information of hon. members, that the court might have taken three different actions in connection with this conviction. It might
have confirmed the conviction; it might have decided that there was some error in law and therefore ordered a new trial; or on the other hand it might have done, what in fact it did in this case, namely, hold that there was no evidence to justify a conviction and decide that the conviction must be quashed.
Now, that is the position in which this man finds himself, and the Postmaster General's department in regarding him as guilty of the charge is simply arrogating to itself the functions of a court of appeal from the appellate division of the Supreme Court of Alberta. The lawyer representing this accused man has been in communication with the Postmaster General's department; I do not think he has been able to get any direct word from the Postmaster General. A letter appears to have been sent under the signature of " T. P. Murphy, private secretary," and I want to direct the attention of the House to portions of it. This letter is dated the 2nd day of February and is addressed to Mr. Hayes' lawyer. It says:
I note you state that the case was appealed and the matter came before the Appeal Court. Mr. Hayes was completely exonerated by two of the judges, the third dissenting. I am given to understand that the quashing of the verdict of the lower court, on appeal being taken, was by reason of" the fact that there was considerable doubt of the guilt of Mr. Hayes in connection with the theft of the letter containing the marked money, but that the judgment did not "completely exonerate" him, as you state. In other words, the appeal was quashed because there was insufficient evidence, and not because it was clearly shown that Mr. Hayes did not commit the theft.
I would ask Mr. Murphy how a court could more fully exonerate an individual than this court did. I must confess that I have never known a case in which a court has held that a person is, to use the language of this letter, completely exonerated. Any exoneration is a complete exoneration, and that is the fact in this case. This private secretary indicates that he is placing his reliance on the judgment of Mr. Justice Clarke, which in substance is the same as the argument used by the Acting Postmaster General, and then he goes on to state:
The circumstances brought out in the evidence show that Mr. Hayes was the only person who would have opportunity, without being observed by others, to steal the test letter containing the marked money, which was subsequently sent by him to the stamp clerk.
Mr. Murphy evidently sets himself up as a judge of the facts and declares that this man is the only one who could have stolen the money, notwithstanding that the Court of Appeal has held that there were numerous individuals who might have been guilty of the offence. I quote further:
Leaving aside technicalities which necessarily enter into a legal trial, the fact remains that Mr. Hayes

Dismissal of John J. Hayes
violated a positive rule of the service in having this letter secreted on his person, and there is strong presumptive evidence that he tampered with it.
Mr. Murphy talks about "technicalities" after the court has found that there was not sufficient evidence to justify the charge against this man. In my opinion Mr. Murphy is guilty of an unwarranted assumption of appellate court functions. He concludes:
In view of the facts above stated, this department cannot, in the public interest, accede to any request that Mr. Hayes be reinstated in the service. The necessity for preserving the safety of the mails entrusted to the care of Post Office employees, makes it impossible, after a careful consideration of all the circumstances in this case, to retain Mr. Hayes in the postal service where he would have access to the mails.
It appears therefore that Mr. Murphy accuses this man of the very crime of which he has been acquitted by the court; and I think that this is a most outrageous letter for an official to send to the lawyer representing an accused person. The government should be the last body to adopt an attitude of this kind towards a humble citizen of this country; and I urge, Mr. Speaker, that ample reparation be made this man. He has been declared innocent; in the eyes of the law he is innocent. If our law is worth anything at all he must therefore be given the benefit of that finding, and in my humble judgment he should be reinstated in his position if he desires to resume it, and should have restored to him the pension privileges of which he has been deprived. I do not think he should be eternally damned in this way and made to suffer for a crime which he never committed and of which the courts in this country have freed him.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: Was there any finding as to the question of the denial of jury?

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
I might elucidate that point which is merely a legal one. Under our Northwest I erritories Act a person who is accused of the crime of theft where the value of the property is under the sum of $200 is not entitled to a jury. That is a provision of the Northwest Territories Act which has not been repealed, and consequently when Mr. Hayes found himself charged with the crime of stealing two dollars he was not entitled to a jury. In addition to that he was liable to a minimum penalty of three years in gaol. The Postmaster General mentioned the fact of his having been sentenced to three years as indicative of the enormity of the offence. Now, no one deprecates these offences more than I do, for we do require honesty in the public service; it is absolutely essential. But I want to direct the Postmaster General's attention to the fact

that the minimum sentence which the court could impose for the offence was three years in gaol; and the man was under our law denied the right of a jury. He was convicted, but that conviction was set aside, and the moment that the conviction was quashed he was innoeent in the eyes of the law. With the setting aside of the conviction the law regarded him as having been innocent at the time the charge was laid. I think it is only fair, Mr. Speaker, that the government, above all organizations, should assume a proper attitude in matters of this kind and not set itself in judgment above the courts of the country; and above all, this man having been found innocent, the government should make ample amends for the injustice, which has been done him.

If there had been only a legal technicality, or if there had' been some doubt as to the value or the significance of the evidence, I doubt not that the Court of Appeal instead of ordering an acquittal would have ordered a new trial. That was not done, and that is the best proof that such evidence as there was was not sufficient to justify the conviction of this man.

Mr. Speaker, the first information I have received of this case is that presented by the hon. members for Calgary (Mr. Irvine and Mr. Shaw). I must say that I find some difficulty in coming to a conclusion on the very brief statement of facts that has been made by the minister as well as by the hon. members to my left. So far as I have been able to gather, one Hayes, an employee of the post office at Calgary, was accused of stealing mail, was brought to trial before Mr. Justice McCarthy, and was by him convicted without a jury, the trial being in every way legal and proper. An appeal was taken to the Appellate Court of Alberta and was heard before Mr. Justice Beck, Mr. APRIL 10, 1923
Dismissal of John J. Hayes
Justice Hyndman and Mr. Justice Clarke. The appeal was on several grounds, but summing up briefly, it resulted in the quashing of the conviction on the ground of insufficiency of evidence, two of the judges being in favour of the quashing and Mr. Justice Clarke dissenting and supporting the conviction by the trial judge. It appears as well that in the judgment of the majority, given by Mr. Justice Beck and supported by Mr. Justice Hyndman, it was found that there were several explanations consistent with the innocence of the accused for the disappearance of the money in queston. The dissenting judge appears to have taken the view that the 'possibility of the money having been stolen by any other person was so remote that it could not be taken into account as overpowering the judgment of facts found by the trial judge.
The Post Office Department, as its conduct is defended by the minister, (Mr. Graham) takes the view that whatever the final judgment, the circumstances affecting the entire case are such that suspicion attaches to the accused, so much so that in the opinion of the department the confidence of the public could not be longer retained in him. The hon. member who has spoken last (Mr. Shaw) urges that the finding of the appellate court must be taken as establishing beyond suspicion the innocence of the accused. While as far as I can gather the facts from the debate, there does seem to be room enough for doubt to justify an acquittal, I would not like to subscribe to the proposition that the government of the country must in its decision of the fitness of an employee for office who has been charged with crime be absolutely bound by the judgment of a court. I feel that a department must be left in a position corresponding with that of the private employer. The private employer would have the right, and in justice to the shareholders of the buisness-if there were such-would be bound to exercise the right, of reviewing all the facts himself and deciding as to the qualifications and fitness of the man for a continuance of trust based upon those facts as they appeared to him.
Now, I have not been convinced that the case is so overwhelmingly in favour of the innocence of Hayes that the department is not justified in exercising its prerogative and saying that "The circumstances are at least so suspicious that we do not think he should be continued in office." It may be that on further argument the case in his favour could be made stronger, but it seems to me that a vote for the amendment is merely a vote
that in all cases the judgment of a court must be final as to the retention of the
4.	p.m. employee. It certainly is final in bo far as it establishes that no proof has been made out of the guilt of the accused, and it is to that extent incumbent on the department, if it feels that his dismissal must take place, to effect it in such a way as to entail as little hardship on him as possible.
It does seem to me strange that Hayes must necessarily be deprived of his pension. I do not know that I got the facts in this special connection right. I understand that he was asked to resign, and declined. I do not think Hayes could have been expected to resign. He appears to have felt himself innocent, he was found innocent by the court, and resignation on his own part upon request by the department would imply something of an admission of guilt. Therefore his refusal to resign should not of itself deprive him of his pension. Though the department may be justified in regarding his case as so surrounded with suspicion that he must not be continued in a post of public trust, the department is bound to put him in a position consistent with his public service. Although for the reasons I have given I purpose voting against the amendment, I would hope that some way could be found of bringing to this man the pension of which I think he should not be deprived because of the final decision of the Court of Appeal.

The government are not going to approach this matter in any niggardly spirit. We are not going to be on easy street as regards money; but we can always get money, and I am not disposed to resort to this merely as a means of getting money. Supply-Labour
to do business much more cheaply than insurance companies, although as a matter of fact, we are selling annuities generally more expensively than they are. I may be wrong, but I believe I am absolutely correct in that statement. What I mean is that you can get better rates from an insurance company paying a dividend than you can from the government which pays no dividend. We should be able to do better than they, because we are under no cost of investment for this scheme. The money all goes into the fund without paying any percentages or commissions or anything else to anybody. We have the money, and there is no expense whatever in connection with the administration of the fund as such. Therefore, again we should be able to do business a little more reasonably and profitably to the people of Canada than insurance companies could.
I appreciate what my hon. friend says as to the difficulty of raising rates. When the four per cent annuity was first started, we had the government borrowing at something like 3J per cent, sometimes 31 per cent, and the idea of the annuity rate was a rate which would yield the annuitant a higher rate than government borrowing would. Ordinarily, that would be the case. Lately, however, we have been in the anomalous position-and I am to blame for it too; I am not criticizing my hon. friend for it at all; we should have taken up this matter before-that we have been actually paying more interest on a thirty-year debenture, at the end of which time the whole capital comes back, than we calculate our annuities at for a much less period. That, of course, is all out of joint; it is all wrong. You cannot expect to do very much with annuities on that basis. I think my hon. friend is right when he says that we are going to have cheaper money. If we get out a number of annuities at a higher rate, we are bound to lose money. While the government ought not to make money in this connection, it ought not to lose money, and therefore we should be careful. While that is quite true as regards long-term annuities, this annuity business can be looked upon as a liquid business, something similar to loans, and a higher rate can be properly applied to short-term annuities. One always pays more for a short-term annuity, and it is money which is just as useful as any other kind of annuity. We know, however, we are going to be paying a high rate of interest for some time ahead, and I would suggest to my hon. friend that he consider an extension of the rate, at least, as regards short-term annuities.

If they indicate their desire to participate in such an investigation, we ask them to name a representative on the board, which presumably the employees have already done, and then ask the two to choose a chairman, and so on. In other words, we help in every way possible to bring about the formation of a board, to delay a strike and bring about an investigation of the differences involved to see if a satisfactory settlement cannot be arrived at. That must be our attitude on all disputes, excepting those which affect public utilities or coal mines. We have under the act, as hon. gentlemen know, no jurisdiction over very many of the disputes that occur from time to time. The Industrial Disputes Investigation Act does not apply in the case of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, but the department has always stood ready and anxious to use its friendly offices and to suggest any possible means of bringing the parties together and getting a thorough discussion of the questions in dispute.

I am not particularly concerned as to who has jurisdiction in this dispute. It may be quite true that the British North America Act makes it difficult for this House, or the department, to act in certain provincial matters; but it does seem to me that the Department of Labour ought to be held responsible for initiating such legislation, or for bringing before the people such measures, as will prevent possible outbreaks in that Nova Scotia district. I think that a great many people have clearly recognized that the conditions there are now rather
fMr. Murdock.]
unique-a huge corporation controlling practically the whole of the industries of that part of the country, there being apparently a small population there and no large body of what has often been termed "neutral opinion". Under these circumstances, the employees are being forced to direct action. A letter was forwarded only a few7 days ago to the Prime Minister which I should like to read, for the information of this committee :
We desire to call your attention to the following facts. Some three weeks ago, Mr. Roy Wolvin, president of the British Empire Steel Corporation, addressed a closed meeting of the Sydney board of trade. His address was of such a character in his own estimation, that although reporters of the local newspapers were present, it was suppressed as being unfit for publication at his request.
However, we have been reliably informed that he stated to the members of the board of trade, that it was up to them to drive the radicals out of Cape Breton, or he would withdraw his capital from this island and allow the grass to grow on the streets of Sydney.
As a direct result of this suppressed speech a second meeting of the board of trade was held in Sydney this present week, an account of which you may find in the Sydney Record of March 28th. The heading of the article reads: "Citizens call for drive to wipe out Bolshevism in Cape Breton". The particular brand of "Bolshevism" which the board of trade is going to stamp out is described as "Cape Breton Bolshevism". The whole resolution breathes the spirit of Mussolini without having the open courage of Mussolini behind it.
"Cape Breton Bolshevism" consists in the working class of Cape Breton employed in the steel works and the coal mines exercising the right handed down to them by their British forefathers to walk off the steel plant to the last man employed and to walk out of the coal mines and leave the directors of the British Empire Steel Corporation to care for these plants as best they may. This right is being exercised in Cape Breton because of the fierce exploitation of labour carried on by the British Empire Steel Corporation.
We are writing this to inform you and your government that ten thousand working men in Cape Breton are accepting the challenge of the Sydney board of trade and are inviting them to start in now and drive out the humblest "Bolshevic" in our ranks. We also demand that a thorough investigation by your government be made into the speech delivered by Wolvin before the Sydney board of trade, which was suppressed.
Copies of this letter are being forwarded to the Hon. E. H. Armstrong, and C. C. Curtis, president of the Sydney Board of Trade.
Yours truly,
Paul McNeil, Secretary,
Steel Workers Union.
J. B. McLachlan, Secretary,
Dis. No. 26 U.M.W. of A.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) and I are surely going to agree on one thing, and that is that this is a serious situation which should be dealt with in some way, and it has been a serious situation for a number of years. But I hope the hon. member will admit the limitations of the federal Department of Labour to deal with the questions involved. The British Empire Steel Corporations is operating, as I understand, under a Nova Scotia charter; the mines, the steel works and the other properties of that company are in the province of Nova Scotia. The disputes that have occurred from time to time have occurred in Nova Scotia, and on every occasion, that the Labour department has had an opportunity to do so, it has indicated a readiness to do, within the law, everything possible to bring about, by investigation or otherwise, a settlement of the controversies. As I said a few days ago, one of the first official acts I was called upon to perform, about the 1st of January, 1922, was to appoint a chairman for a board of investigation in regard to the coal mine situation in Nova Scotia, which board had been authorized and established and was waiting the appointment of a chairman when this government took office., It is not necessary to go into a discussion of what developed out of that investigation. Some members might very truthfully say to me-and I would not dispute it if they did-that worse than nothing came out of the investigation held in the early part of 1922. But is that. to be charged to the Labour department? Is that to be charged to this government? Is therq any coercive right vested in the Labour department or in this government that gives us authority to say "Thou shalt" or "Thou shalt not" to either employer or employee? If there is I know nothing of it. But still it is very easy, in fact it is customary, when any dispute develops in any part of the country, in any walk of life, to turn to the federal Labour department, which may not have, under the law, anything to do with it, and to criticize that department for its omissions or its commissions in the matter.
I am sure' my hon. friends will recognize the fact that we have in Canada nine provinces, most of which have Labour departments with certain duties, functions and rights, that the Labour department of the federal government has only the rights conceded to it under the law and, that it is ready and willing to do anything it can to bring about thorough investigation with a view to the settlement of the disputes.
In regard to the particular situation that my hon. friend speaks of in Nova Scotia, what do we find at the present moment? What might be termed a club is held over the heads of the people of Nova Scotia, by labour, it is said. In other words, it has been indicated that a strike is going to occur on the 1st day of April unless 30 per cent increased compensation be granted, unless an eight-hour day be conceded and unless a check-off system be recognized by the employing company. As the Labour department of the federal government we might be interested in that, but I would like any hon. member to indicate to me how, in any particular, we can interfere and say "Thou shalt" or "Thou shalt not" to either employer or employee concerned. In other words, we have absolute limitations that I hope my hon. friends will appreciate before holding, as people are sometimes too ready to do, the Labour department responsible for all the disputes that are inevitable.
In the case of the Nova Scotia situation, as soon as the Labour department heard the proposal that a strike was likely to occur on the 1st day of April, one of the most capable and experienced officers of the department was sent down to Sydney, to suggest that the friendly offices of the department, through an investigation or in any other consistent way under the law, were available for the use of the workmen concerned, and we were given to understand that the men and committees were amply sufficient by themselves to deal with the matter. That is the situation that we find ourselves in as regards certain industrial disputes that we have no jurisdiction over.

speechtext: Has the province of Nova Scotia a Labour department?

Supply-Labour

department would feel freer to act in the discussion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE

Where there was not a separate Labour department, we might find ourselves approaching someone not so sympathetic to the question of a Labour department, and possibly more taken up with the operation of some other particular department.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: Is it within the power of the Dominion government, according to the Minister of Labour, to make a thorough investigation of conditions which prevail in Cape Breton, to go thoroughly into the question of the British Empire Steel Corporation, its finances, the hold it has on the country, its connections with steel companies south of the line, the control exerted over its policies by the United States companies? maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE

speechtext:
I understood the minister to say that the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act had application to coal mines, railways and certain public utilities. one in the history of my experience in Simcoe. I was wondering where the minister gets the authority for that statement.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: I might give a concrete example. Right at the present moment we have in course of formation a board of conciliation for a gas works in a certain city in the Dominion of Canada. maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
It may be that there is some amendment that I am not familiar with, but section 5 of the act reads:
Wherever any dispute exists between an employer and any of his employees, and the parties thereto are unable to adjust it, either of the parties to the dispute may make application to the minister for the appointment of a board of conciliation and investigation, to which board the dispute may be referred under the provisions of this act.
It is true there is in that section a proviso which specifically deals with railway companies, but I do not think that would warrant the statement of the minister. I am not saying he is wrong; I do not know. If he is right, it might be proper to consider an extension of the act. If again the reason that the act is not extended is because of property and civil rights, how then can there be any jurisdiction regarding a coal mine which is located in one province? I imagine in most cases the operations of a coal mine in a province are pursuant to a charter issued by that province. If the objection is that property and civil rights belong exclusively to the province, I do not see why a coal mine would come within the provisions of the act. At all events there are the two propositions. That is one, and the other is: What limitation is there to the wide-open provisions of section 5 of the act?

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
To deal with the point that is now before us, we should turn to section 2 of the act and read the definition of employer:
"Employer" means any person, company or- corporation employing ten. or more persons and owing or operating any mining property, agency of transportation or communication, or public service utility, including, except as hereinafter provided, railways, whether operated by steam, electricity or other motive power, steamships, telegraph and telephone lines, gas, electric light, water and power works, or any number of such persons, companies or corporations acting together, or who in the opinion of the minister have interest in common.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
What can. the Department of Labour do in case of an industrial dispute? What is its power?

Supply-Labour

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: That is a very large order from my hon. friend. If both employer and employees adopt the same attitude in a controversy-that is certain individuals presuming to speak for employers at times and certain individuals presuming to speak for employees at times-the Labour department can do absolutely nothing; they are powerless under any legal rights that at present a Labour department would have. The Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, as I think has been very aptly suggested, is only for the purpose of bringing the parties together to reason, thresh out and determine as between each other their mutual differences with a view of arriving, if possible, at a mutually satisfactory understanding. It might be very aptly described as an intended league of industry and labour. But if either industry or labour or both bow their necks and go around with a chip on their shoulders and are ready to fight first, last and all the time, then this league of nations in a modified form would be absolutely useless. In a few cases in the past where this disposition has been shown by certain individuals this league has proved absolutely useless in preventing discord and strikes as a result of disputes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: Do I understand the reasoning of the minister in this regard to be that if employees are firm in their demand and if employees through their representatives are equally firm in *heirs, so that there is a deadlock, then the department can do nothing? If there is a disposition on the part of the contending parties to come to an agreement they , do not need government assistance. maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
If my hon. friend only
had a little experience in connection with the aims, ambitions and contentions of labour he would not make any such statement as we have just heard. We find that since 1907 there have been 597 applications made for boards of investigation, not by individuals, either employers or employees, who were ready, as my hon. friend suggests, to bow their necks and not do anything, but by citizens of Canada who were presumably desirous of reaching common ground with those opposed to them in the particular disputes. As 1 say,
597 applications were made, and 428 boards have been granted under the law during the period I have mentioned. takes the view that I suggested that the act was not of any value. maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: I would say that the minister was badly advised in basing the interpretation of the powers of the act on the 36 cases in which a settlement was not reached, and in omitting to mention the 400 odd cases in which it operated.

I may say that the items as read will probably not conform to the expenditure this year, for it is very doubtful if it will be possible to have the plans completed and the stone cutting done in time to carry on the erection of the tower to completion.
But from this item there will be an expenditure to cover the settlement with the architects. A settlement has been reached recently whereby payment will be made to
9	p.m. them for the balance of their commission on the work that has been done to date. For the information of the committee I will give a short review of the conclusions that we have arrived at in making a settlement with the architects: The total expenditure on the buildings to November 28th was $9,910,972. Mr. Pearson's commission on that amount at 4f per cent would be $458,382.48.
We have not settled on that basis. We have followed to some extent the line suggested by the parliamentary committee, and we did make an adjustment with the architects in 1921 when they were allowed certain commissions on an expenditure over and above $5,000,000. There is no doubt that when the parliament buildings contract was entered into there was a desire and an effort made to limit the expenditure to some $5,000,000 but as the work proceeded alterations took place, the designs were changed, and in 1920 we find that the expenditure had exceeded the limitation of $5,000,000 by over $1,034,000; in January, 1921, the expenditure had amounted to $7,966,000, and on November 1, 1921, it had amounted to $9,157,229. The original plans

Supply-Public IPorfcs
as suggested by the architect, and desires probably of the committee were changed, with the result that this larger expenditure was made on the buildings that we are now occupying. Some of that increased cost, in fact, a considerable proportion of it can be accounted for by the increase in the cost of material and labour that took place during the years between 1918 and 1921, but in addition to that, the buildings as originally designed have been changed, accounting for an additional expenditure.
So far as the architects are concerned, they did originally indicate by letter that they would design and construct a building limited in cost to $5,000,000, and on receipt of their letter accepting the above offer and stating that the terms there set forth were satisfactory to them, a contract was prepared by the department with a limitation fee. . When the contract was presented to the architects they took exception to the limitation in a letter dated July 6, 1916. Although that contract was presented it was never executed, the architects stating that they could not agree to the clause limiting the fee as no such limitation had ever been discussed with the committee. They acknowledged acceptance of the terms of the joint committee in which the limitation of fee was made, but stated that their acceptance was an inadvertence so far as the limitation of fee was concerned, it being intended to apply to the other conditions only.

speechtext: What date was that?

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
In 1916. Although the architects did not sign this contract, the work continued, and as I have pointed out in the year 1920 the limitation of $5,000,000 was exceeded, further exceeded in 1921, and by November, 1921, the cost had amounted to $9,157,229. In the year 1920 the architects did complain and ask that they be given further consideration in regard to the overexpenditure. The department under instructions from the committee had Mr. Ewart, the Consulting Architect, make an examination of the building to try and indicate wherein the plans had been altered and new works undertaken, and to estimate the additional amount that might be paid to the architects. Mr. Ewart reported an amount of $1,396,999 as-representing extra work and stated that further consideration of various items would be necessary before a final estimate could be arrived at of the value of the extra work done up to January 31, 1921. Unfortunately Mr. Ewart became ill and died, and Mr. Sutherland was then employed to report further on
109i
these additional items, and he found an amount of $337,401 that might be attributed to extra work. The committee at that time recommended and did pay an extra commission on $1,734,401.13. This estimate as compared with an estimate presented by the architects showed that the committee did not allow the full amount. In other words, the architects claim that they should have received in addition to the commission on $1,734,401.13, an additional commission on $946,277.
In December, 1921, Mr. Pearson was still urging further consideration of his claim. The then outgoing minister advised him that it would be necessary for this matter to be dealt with by the incoming administration. The architect at that time advised the minister that it would be necessary for him to close down the works. In a letter written on December 21, 1921, he advised the then minister that he had no alternative but to close down the work and that he would issue instructions to that effect to the general contractor, and on the same date he wrote to the general contractor giving him instructions to close down the works at the end of the week. I merely mention that as a matter of information for the committee. Mr. Pearson at that time felt it was necessary for him to retire from the work, and since that date he has not been associated directly with it. In fact, as is well known, there has not been any large undertaking since that date. The matter of adjusting the differences between the architects and the department was one presenting some difficulties. I think, generally speaking, that those who have followed the construction of the building and who have knowledge of the original intentions of the committee and of what has transpired since, will realize that there was a further obligation by parliament to the architects in the matter of payment for their work in connection with these buildings. That was recognized by the parliamentary committee and payments made as I have indicated.
We have taken up the situation where we found it in 1921 and with the aid of three hon. members of this House-the hon. member for London, the hon. member for Brandon and the hon. member for St. Lawrence and St. George-who have acted with myself and members of the department in bringing about what we considered a fair and reasonable adjustment of this claim we have arrived at the conclusion that the architects would be entitled to a payment of commission on $9,910.,972.59 less a deduction on account of increased cost not allowed on $1,683,463.46. In other words the commissions payable to Mr. Pear-
Supply-Public Works

son would amount to a total sum of $458,382- less a credit of 4f on $1,683,463.46 of $77,860, or a commission of $380,522.30 plus a fee for work of a special character of 2J per cent on $932,960.74, or a commission of $31,822.62 plus a sum of $5,000 allowed for advertising and receiving tenders for special furniture and special work; making a total commision of $412,344 to Mr. Pearson, with a credit of payments received of $289,340, leaving a balance due Mr. Pearson of $123,004.20. Mr. Mar-chand's settlement is worked out on the same basis, he being allowed a commission of \ of one per cent on the total, his total commission being $71,199, and he having received payment of $52,848, leaving a balance of $19,142. That is the settlement that has been entered into with the architects and an agreement has been made as the result of which there will be no overlapping of commissions. It will be a complete and distinct settlement. For the completion of this building it is hoped that we will be able to enter into a contract that will be distinct and separate from the old contract. This settlement of $142,000 will be paid out of the vote of $700,000 that is now before the committee. I think this statement pretty well explains the item of $700,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: Last year representations were made that some change should be made in the arrangement of this chamber in order to improve the acoustics. Some changes have been made that have effected a considerable improvement. Last lyear the minister said that he would look into the matter and see if the Speaker's Chair could be moved down on one side and the seating rearranged so that members could hear better than they can at the present time. While improvements have been made, the acoustics of this chamber are very poor. I would personally feel like fining the architect if he was responsible for designing this chamber because the designing was very poorly done for an assembly of this size. This assembly will increase in numbers as time goes on. In fact, after the next general election we shall have an increase, and it is quite possible that it will be in this section of the House. maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
We had certain
investigations made after last session as regards the acoustics, and we were advised to carry on the scheme as hon. members see it before them, that is, of placing felt and carpet on the floor, and the hanging of draperies and curtains. I think it is evident to all members that a great and satisfactory improvement has been made by this simple expenditure. We also had models made, and I think I shall have them brought to the House and placed where members can see them, showing a rearrangement of seating and the placing of the Speaker in the centre of the chamber. Since the changes have been made during the interval and in view of the success of those changes, my view

and I think this is the view of many members with whom I have discussed the matter-is that we should not disturb the present arrangement, but possibly carry a little further next year the scheme as carried on last summer. It has been suggested that in and around the upper balconies further draperies or coverings might be placed which will tend to absorb the vibrations or voice sounds and probably add to the acoustic properties of the chamber. Personally, I am fairly well satisfied. I think in a chamber of this character, of this height and extent, the members are probably not suffering a great deal to-day, and that those who are accustomed to speaking and who speak clearly and distinctly do not have great difficulty in being heard. It would be a mistake to rearrange the seating; moretyer, it has been estimated that to carry out a scheme of that kind would cost about $45,000, and at the present time, I would not feel disposed to ask that a change of that kind be made.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
I would like to make one suggestion as regards improving this House as a chamber for discussion and speaking. That would be to take the four front seats on the middle of each side and let those be made a bench where members could go to make set speeches whenever they wished to be heard in all parts of the House. A minister making a statement on behalf of the government involving the policy of the government or of his department could thus speak from the centre of the chamber, and if somebody on this side wished to criticise him, he could speak from the centre also, if he had an argument he wished, not only the House, but the country to hear. We have been spending a good deal of money to improve the acoustics of this chamber and such a change would cost very little. I have several times felt that I could, perhaps, put my case a little more clearly if I could sit nearer the
Supply-Public Works

centre. There are plenty of other seats left; the whole of the chamber is not occupied, and such a change as I have suggested would not inconvenience anyone but would be a great improvement and might lead also to improvement in the character of the debates. If we had such a speaking bench on either side of the chamber, this would not involve an expenditure of $1,000. It would not change the character of the chamber; but it would improve it as a chamber of discussion and speaking, so that everybody could hear, especially those who had something important to say and who were willing to go to the centre of the House to say it in order that they might be heard by the members and that their speeches might be in a better shape to go to the country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
I should like to hear from some of the members who sit at the far end of the chamber, how much they have heard of the minister's explanation of this item and of the discussion that has been going on at this end. I remember the time when I sat at the far end of the chamber. There were ten of us in that little group and there were days when we never heard one thing in regard to the estimates that were being considered. All we knew about them was what we read the next day in Hansard. I realize the very great disadvantage under which hon. members are placed in that end of the chamber. maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: Of course, we have the original draft of plan showing the elevation, and in addition to that models have been prepared which I have no doubt were photographed, as my hon, friend says. maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: There is one thing the minister can do for hon. members and it will not cost anyone a cent, while it will make for much more livable conditions in this chamber. maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: It is cold air?

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE

speechtext:
At present we are depending on nothing.

speechtext: Personally I am not disposed to spend a great deal of money.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
It seems to me that the original estimated cost of the building and the actual cost to date are so much at variance that we ought to have a fuller explanation from the minister as to how the difference came about. We are all aware that the committee of seven gentlemen in charge of the work was composed of some of the ablest men in the House on both sides of politics, as well as of gentlemen
from the Senate; and as the matter stands today it seems to reflect more or less on the work of that committee. I have not the details, but I remember distinctly that when the restoration of the building was first under contemplation it was said that the old walls would be utilized, and later it was decided to put on an extra storey. I asked the minister definitely whether the $5,000,000 estimated cost included the tearing down of walls and the putting up of new walls, in addition to the extra storey, and he said he thought it did.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: Who was the minister at that time?

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: I am not criticizing any minister.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: No, but I am asking for information.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: At this moment I cannot recall, but I suppose it was the Hon. Robert Rogers, although I am not positive. But it makes no difference who it was, he was one of the seven. There can be no doubt that any changes that were decided upon were first investigated by the architect and submitted to the committee, and in the end, I believe, received its endorsation. I am aware that the Postmaster General (Mr. Murphy) withdrew for some reason, but so far as I know the other members of the committee were unanimous in regard to the changes made from time to time. I think it is due the House that a full explanation should be given by the minister as to exactly what was under contemplation when the estimate of $5,000,000 was given, and how it was that the figure rose from that sum to 810,000,000. The minister has been quite fair. He has pointed out that a considerable proportion of the increase was due to increased cost of material and labour, but I hardly think that this would account for the whole increase, and I am sure the House will be interested to get a fuller explanation of the matter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
A few moments ago I gave briefly some of the information my hon. friend is now requesting. But so that the committee may have fuller information I would read from this report:
Mr. John A. Pearson, architect, Toronto, Ontario, and Mr. J. O. Marchand, architect, Montreal, Que., were instructed by Hon. Mr. Rogers, then Minister of Public Works, to report on the condition of the ruins of the parliament buildings as they stood after the fire, and the report of these architects was presented to the Minister of Public Works on the 17th February, 1916.
The architects stated that the ruins of the building as it stood represented in labour and materials an
Supply-Public Works

asset of $2,000,000. This estimate with the architect's
detail is as follows:
The new west wing	 $ 425,000
The library building valued at	 650,000
The boiler room, heating plant in basement and chimney stack, all of which would represent a value of about	 1,000,000
I find my impression was right when I said at first that I thought the value was between one and two million dollars.
Messrs. Pearson and Marchand were instructed to prepare sketch plans for the reconstruction of the parliament buildings. These were submitted to the committee, and after discussion it was considered advisable in rebuilding the structure to provide greater accommodation than existed in the old building. The architects were requested to prepare sketch plans showing an additional storey.
There was an additional storey.
Mr. Pearson submitted these plans at a subsequent meeting of the reconstruction committee and pointed out in discussing them that the addition of another storey would necessitate the taking down of the upper storey of the building, also the main tower. The committee carefully considered the matter and it was finally decided to add the extra storey to the building.
The plans for the layout of the building were submitted to the members of the Senate and House of Commons on two or three occasions, and it was explained to them that in order to carry out the scheme it was necessary to tear down the recently erected west wing and all the walls standing north and in the rear of the external south walls and the east and west pavilions; this was in order that the two chambers, the Senate and House of Commons, might be placed at the extreme east and west ends respectively of the new building so that they would have outside light. It was also decided, in order to reduce the danger from fire, to make the building as fireproof as possible and remove the boilers and heating plant to a central heating station outside of the building.
A report from the architects, dated July 29, 1916, was subsequently submitted to the committee dealing with the reasons for demolishing the walls of the old Parliament Buildings which were left standing after the fire; the architect explaining that several sketch plans were prepared in an endeavour to have the Commons chamber within the area of the block so as to retain the west wing, but it was impossible to get a properly balanced plan and the idea had ultimately to be discarded as the architects were convinced that no satisfactory scheme could be arrived at by endeavouring to tack the building on the west wing. They further stated that no portion of the walls above the foundation of the west wing could be used. The foundations of the remaining portion of the south or front wall were built of inferior masonry and the architects considered it better to tear out this masonry, and the wisdom of this decision was proved when they discovered stretches of the wall in the centre had been built of dry rubble.
I think that gives a fairly clear explanation of what led up to the destruction of the old walls.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: Is the minister reading from the minutes of the committee?

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
Were minutes kept?
fMr. J. H. King.]

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: It is a summary from the minutes of the committee as prepared by the estimate clerk for the information of the committee. I think it covers everything pretty fully. This report was made in July, 1916, after the old walls had beer taken down, and the estimate of the new building was fixed at $5,000,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: Do the minutes show what members of the committee were present when that was agreed upon, and whether or not there were any dissenting voices?

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: I have not the minutes of the committee. Of course, they are very extensive, many meetings having been held. I am not sure whether the minutes would show that information, but I have no doubt they would confirm what I have stated to the committee.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: It would seem to me in view certainly of the implied, if not actual, criticism that it is important to know whether the committee was unanimous, or whether this work was forced on, so to speak, by a majority of the committee against the views of the other members. If so I have never heard of it, and I have been a member of the House for all these years.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: Did the members of the reconstruction committee receive any remuneration besides their indemnities?

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: Were they supposed to stay on the job all the year round and look after this work at their own expense?

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-DISMISSAL OF JOHN J. HAYES FROM POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
Then it looks to me as if the reconstruction committee were not expected to exercise very much supervision over the building of this structure the year round, and this impression is strengthened by the discussion we have had. In fact the architects and contractors were left largely to themselves. Due to the fact that the contract was on a cost plus basis and that no very close supervision was exercised by the reconstruction committee, the government or anyone else in authority except the architects, it is my candid opinion that herein lies the reason for the very high cost of construction. I am not blaming the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. King). I think he has had a very undesirable legacy bequeathed to him. I do not know just where to place the blame, but I think this committee should know where the fault lies, because already the country has spent more money than should have been spent for the value received.
